own_scenes.desc: Dimitri Hegemann, harto del rock suicida de Berlín, creó a mediados de los ochenta el laboratorio dadaísta Fischbüro, el sello Interfisch y los festivales de ruido Atonal, donde la última edición juntó a The Final Cut con 808 State y Baby Ford. En 1991 el sello Tresor arrancó con un EP de X-101, proyecto de UR, y en 1992 publicó X-102 Discovers the Rings of Saturn: el eje Detroit-Berlín.

notes.chapter: Cap. 6: Applied Technology: The Myth of Techno Collides with Reality, 1991–2001
notes.text: Tras la caída del Muro (noviembre de 1989), la tierra de nadie de Potsdamer Platz quedó vacía; en 1991 Hegemann y los de Interfisch encontraron las cámaras acorazadas con barrotes del desaparecido almacén Wertheim y abrieron allí el club Tresor («caja fuerte»), donde se juntaron chavales del Este y del Oeste con un estilo orientado al Detroit mínimo. Revivió carreras de Detroit (Santonio Echols, Eddie Fowlkes, Blake Baxter, junto a Dr. Motte y Tanith); el recopilatorio Tresor II: Berlin-Detroit: A Techno Alliance (1993, NovaMute) selló la alianza, y hasta se planeó un Tresor en Detroit. Su agente Alexandra Dröner bromeaba con el «tekno con cuatro kas» antes de volverse militante del origen de Detroit. Berlín se convirtió en el segundo centro lógico del techno y en la capital musical de Alemania.

refs.q: An X-101 EP went on to launch the German label Tresor in 1991, which also released X-102’s legendary 1992 album X-102 Discovers the Rings of Saturn.
refs.para: Two of the first projects nurtured under the Submerge umbrella were UR conceptual side projects—X-101 and X-102. An X-101 EP went on to launch the German label Tresor in 1991, which also released X-102’s legendary 1992 album X-102 Discovers the Rings of Saturn. Saturn was no ordinary concept album, at least not by the same prog-rock standards the term implies. The album featured fourteen songs, each named after the planet’s rings and moons, with track lengths (and subsequently track widths on the vinyl copies) corresponding to the actual sizes of and distances between the celestial bodies.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Off to Battle: Redefining the Detroit Underground, 1990–1995

refs.q: Recalls Hegemann, “We were the place where East and West kids came together, musically. We found our style—it was definitely oriented toward minimal Detroit sounds, and then after a year and half we had our own crowd.”
refs.para: The area around the wall that had traditionally separated East from West still existed as a sort of “no-man’s-land,” and the buildings in the area remained largely unoccupied through the nearly year-long reunification process. By 1991, however, Potsdamer Platz had a new resident: Hegemann and Co. While searching for a new club location, the former Interfisch crew had stumbled on a series of underground rooms with iron bars, which had once served as vaults for the now-defunct Wertheim department store (once the largest store in Europe). The group’s new club became known as Tresor, a German word meaning “vault” or “safe.” It was an unlikely but incredible place to start. Recalls Hegemann, “We were the place where East and West kids came together, musically. We found our style—it was definitely oriented toward minimal Detroit sounds, and then after a year and half we had our own crowd.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 6: Applied Technology: The Myth of Techno Collides with Reality, 1991–2001

refs.para: Hegemann was intent on building a connection between Berlin and Detroit, as evidenced from the 1993 compilation Tresor II: Berlin-Detroit: A Techno Alliance, made available to U.S. audiences through NovaMute. There were even plans to open a Tresor club in Detroit, which eventually fizzled out. Says Hegemann, “Musically, we had this help from Detroit, and after a while we thought we’d give something back. I thought it was a good challenge. There are so many possibilities [in Detroit] and I thought something could be done. Why is Detroit still asleep?”
